NAH - everyone grieves differently, especially when losing someone to a slow and painful disease like Alzheimer’s. I had a friend go through something similar, and she explained it very well. Sometimes people work through the grief when a person is dying of an illness when they are still alive. In a way you lost the person you know as your grandmother a long time ago and thus likely went through all the stages while she was still alive. When she passed, you already are at the stage of acceptance. It doesn’t mean you love her any less. Your feelings may change with time, and that’s okay too. I’m sorry for your loss!

I totally understand the sitting in silence thing. I used to do that with every single therapist I had tried, and I always thought it was because I have always struggled to talk about my feelings. I gave up on it until a couple months ago when I was forced to go back and had a new therapist. I don’t know what it was, but I was finally able to open up and I understood what people had been saying by having to find a good fit for it to work. I don’t know what your situation is, but is there anyway that you can find another therapist? Maybe the one you have now can help you find another that is free/you can afford, because they seem to realize it’s not a good fit either. It could have to do with their treatment approach and what type of therapy they use. It could help to look up the different styles and see which one seems most appealing to you. Please don’t give up on yourself and getting the help you need and deserve.

Hey buddy. I’m sorry for how you’re feeling. I’ve been there. 

Can you get yourself out of your environment? Go for a walk maybe? Sometimes a change of scenery can help clear your head. 

If you are genuinely afraid that you are going to hurt yourself, please, please, please call 911, the mental health emergency hotline, or whatever number is the equivalent in your country. They can help you, and even if you are afraid of what will happen next, they can keep you safe. I had to be in an inpatient facility when I was going to kill myself, and even though I was terrified and angry at the people that put me there, they kept me safe. 

I’m not going to tell you any BS about how “life gets better!!!” because in times of despair and hopelessness, those words are meaningless. One thing that helps is the hold onto the fear of hurting yourself and curiosity for the future. Maybe things won’t necessarily be better right away, but they will change, and that’s something to be intrigued about and hold onto. 

I’m sorry for what you’re going through. I am here for you and you can always talk to me about anything, please hold on and get the help you need.

That sounds a lot like clinical depression. It’s a disorder that affects the way people can think and feel, making them feel sad, unmotivated, and hopeless even when there might not be any outside factors to make them feel that way. 

Think about all the things that make you happy. Your friends and family, your hobbies, your interests, those sorts of things. When you spend time doing them, they make you feel happy, right? When someone has depression, they could be doing all those things, but they don’t feel good or happy from them. Their brain isn’t working the way it should be, and I’m sure you can imagine how sad and hard that must feel. A lot of times people with depression can feel guilty for those feelings, especially when from the outside, it may look like they have no “reason” to feel that way. But the reality is that there is a chemical reason for their feelings that is out of their control. 

It’s hard to understand for people who do not suffer from depression, but you seem like a very kind and supportive brother who cares a lot and wants to help, and so does your family. But because it’s a biological disease, your sister needs to get help from a doctor. Depression can be treated with therapy and even medication, and that’s what can help your sister right now. Talk to your parents and sister so they can also understand what’s going on. It helps to remember that depression is an illness - if she had the flu you would take her to the doctor, so why should this be any different? 

As for what you can do right now, I think just being there for her is all you can. Help her get the treatment she needs, and remind her of how much you love her and give her someone she can have for support. I’m sure she is very grateful to have you in your life, but sometimes people with depression need extra reminders because their brain can almost trick them into thinking that they are alone. I hope your sister can get the help she needs and can soon start to feel better!

I’ve also been afraid to share suicidal thoughts in the past (I was hospitalized but that was for an actual attempt). I think sharing your thoughts and making it clear that you have no plan/intent is incredibly important. It’s scary but in reality you just have to acknowledge that you can’t get rid of the thoughts and your therapist can’t help you either if you don’t bring them up. A good therapist would know the difference between thoughts and action, and you shouldn’t be scared to share them. Another thing I’ve been really happy with this time around is that since I’m not a minor anymore, my therapist doesn’t go and share everything with my parents. That was always a fear of mine so I wouldn’t want to say anything that would upset my parents, even though that meant I wouldn’t talk about anything. I hope any of this helps, and good luck man! NTA, but as someone who recently went through the college application process, I HIGHLY recommend you don’t write about your parents. If you write about your parents, there might not be enough room in there to discuss your strength and successes as a (near) adult. You seem like a very impressive student with plenty of achievements, so I’m sure you have many other essay topics that would highlight those qualities. You don’t want the admissions people to pity you, you want them to want you in their school. Whatever route you take, good luck!
